newsitem.title: UK: Britain denies it stalling N. Irish peace efforts.
newsitem.headline: Britain denies it stalling N. Irish peace efforts.

text.p: Britain denied on Friday it was stalling peace efforts in Northern Ireland, saying it would set up a commission "very soon" to help settle the contentious issue of sectarian parades.

But both tension and violence were building up ahead of yet another of the many anniversaries that set off trouble in the province -- this one marking a year since the IRA abandoned its ceasefire with a bomb attack on London's Canary Wharf district.
The weekend could also be troublesome if Protestants go ahead with a protest march outside a Roman Catholic Church they have been picketing for months in the town of Harryville.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring voiced concern about the weekend in a meeting on Thursday night with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew.

"We raised concerns over what has been happening over many months in Harryville. I think it is fair to say that protests and pickets outside places of worship are unacceptable in any community in Northern Ireland," Spring told reporters.

Spring said he was disappointed that Britain had failed to implement the recommendations of an independent commission on Northern Ireland's marches, which last year sparked violent protest across the province.

"We have not been encouraged by the British government's indication that it will begin only a partial implementation of the recommendations, despite widespread support for it at Westminster," Spring said before the talks. But Mayhew denied the British were stalling.
"A commission will be appointed very, very soon to look at marching, to help conciliation, to help people get together, to help people make local agreements," he told BBC radio on Friday.

"That's going to be put in place straight away," he added. "Nothing takes priority over local agreements and it is because of local fears, local antagonisms, local conflicting traditions that we have this trouble."

Escalating IRA violence has fuelled fears across Northern Ireland's deeply divided Unionist and Nationalist parties that pro-British Loyalist extremists might abandon a truce they called in October 1994 in response to an IRA ceasefire.
The twin ceasefires fed hopes that the province might escape a quarter-century of bloodshed over British rule.
But optimism has faded since Irish Republican Army guerrillas renewed their destructive campaign one year ago.

Two British soldiers escaped injury just outside Belfast's international airport on Friday morning when someone shot at them. A police spokesman said an unmarked military vehicle was struck by three bullets fired by unknown attackers.
"The two occupants -- both soldiers -- were unhurt and did not stop," the spokesman said.
On Thursday British forces arrested 11 people in Belfast and Lurgan in a counter-insurgency operation. Late on Thursday a small bomb was thrown at a police vehicle in Lurgan but no one was hurt.

And hours before, soldiers found an IRA-type mortar apparently dumped behind houses in the town. Police said that had it been fired at a military vehicle, a likely target, soldiers would have been killed.
Mayhew said the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein would continue to be shut out of talks on the future of the province if such incidents continued.
"They blew apart the process which would have had them around the table a year ago," he told the BBC.
